bio.en: Jag Duggal is Chief Product Officer at Nubank, the massively under-the-radar Brazilian fintech with a fanatical user base that is larger than Coinbase, Robinhood, Affirm, SoFi, and Lemonade combined; before Nubank he led product at Facebook, Google, and Quantcast.
bio.zh: Jag Duggal 是 Nubank 的首席产品官；Nubank 是一家极度低调却庞大的巴西金融科技公司，拥有狂热的用户群，规模超过 Coinbase、Robinhood、Affirm、SoFi 和 Lemonade 之和；加入 Nubank 前，他曾在 Facebook、Google 和 Quantcast 领导产品。

summary.en: Jag explains how Nubank wins not by being incrementally better but fundamentally different, earning fanatical love (80–90% of growth is word of mouth) and only scaling a product line once its Sean Ellis score crosses a compelling threshold. He discusses how to develop a clear strategy (channeling Kevin Systrom's 'at least we are clear'), category design, and disciplined product-line expansion into lending, investing, insurance, and small business. The conversation is a masterclass in building products people love and in the future of FinTech out of Latin America.
summary.zh: Jag 解释了 Nubank 何以胜出：不是“好一点”，而是“根本不同”，从而赢得狂热的喜爱（80%–90% 的增长来自口碑），并且只有当某个产品线的 Sean Ellis 分数越过有说服力的门槛后才会扩张。他谈到了如何制定清晰的战略（借鉴 Kevin Systrom 的“至少我们是清晰的”）、品类设计，以及向借贷、投资、保险和小企业业务的有纪律的品类扩张。这期对话是关于“打造人们热爱的产品”以及拉美金融科技未来的公开课。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It feels like NewBank is one of the historically most successful companies that launching new business lines.

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: We built a lending product, we built an investment product, we built an insurance product, we built a series of small business products. We rarely scale a project until we know the Sean Ellis score hit a threshold that we find really compelling.
turns.zh: 我们开发了贷款产品、投资产品、保险产品，还有一系列面向小企业的产品。在项目规模化之前，我们总会先确保Sean Ellis评分达到我们认为足够有吸引力的阈值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about strategy.
turns.zh: 我想谈谈战略问题。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Kevin Systrom in the early days of Instagram, I heard him say it at a conference. We may not be right, but at least we are clear. Even if your strategy isn't right, you have a very clear idea of what was supposed to be happening.
turns.zh: 早期Instagram的创始人凯文·西斯特罗姆（Kevin Systrom）在一次会议上说过一句话：“我们可能做得不对，但至少思路清晰。即便战略有偏差，你也能清楚知道原本应该怎么做。”

turns.zh: 我倍感荣幸。感谢你们的到来。我想先分享一些关于NewBank的数据，我相信这些会让大家惊叹不已。我觉得很多美国人对NewBank都知之甚少，而这场对话将帮助听众们更加关注我们即将讨论的内容和分享的经验。（00:05:02）：首先，NewBank的规模比Coinbase、Robinhood、Affirm、SoFi和Lemonade加起来还要大。NewBank 80%到90%的增长来自口碑推荐。第三，NewBank的客户数量超过了美国四大银行之一的美国银行，而该银行目前仅在拉丁美洲的三个国家开展业务。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like that that's a record no one can break because it was the first one. That's a sneaky way to get a record. That's hilarious. So my sense is the reason that NewBank thrived and made it is, there's this obsession with building a product that customers are fanatical about. The stat that I shared of 80% to 90% of growth is word of mouth. And this idea of growing through word of mouth in this way is the dream of every company, whether you're consumer business, B2B, a bank especially, very unlikely that you grow at this rate through word of mouth. (00:06:24): So I want to try to help people learn from what you guys have figured out about how to drive such massive word of mouth growth. And maybe just to start from the product perspective, how do you build a product team and a product development process that enables you to build a product that people get fanatical about. And just want to tell all their friends about?
turns.zh: 我觉得这个纪录没人能打破，因为它是首个纪录。这真是偷懒打破纪录的绝佳方法，太搞笑了。在我看来，NewBank成功的原因在于，他们痴迷于打造让客户为之疯狂的产品。我分享的数据显示，80%到90%的增长来自口碑推荐。通过这种方式实现口碑增长是每个公司的梦想，无论是消费品业务、B2B公司还是银行，都很难通过口碑实现如此高速增长。（00:06:24）：所以我想帮助大家从你们的成功中汲取经验，学习如何推动如此大规模的口碑增长。或许先从产品角度入手，你们是如何组建产品团队和产品开发流程的，从而打造出让用户为之疯狂、迫不及待想向朋友安利的产品？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah, I think there are a few things that are the fundamentals of making that happen. And to be clear, a lot of this predates my joining the company a little short of five years ago, but I think is an incredible story and is part of what inspired me to join. But first I would say, really think hard and tap into a very deep pain point. The large incumbent Brazilian banks were amongst the most profitable in the world, they were also amongst the most hated in the world. (00:07:20): And my personal experience with that is early in my career, 20 years earlier in the late '90s, I had done a consulting project in Sao Paulo. And I remember walking to lunch one day with the client, who's a friend of mine, and we were going to Classic Churrasque Korea in Sao Paulo. And we were walking by his bank branch, and we were at a stoplight, and he basically said, that's my bank and I hate them. It was 1997. (00:07:50): And it always stuck in my head. It stuck in my head for 20 years later when David first reached out to me. So we were tapping into a deep pain point, we can go into exactly why. But that was one thing. The second thing that I would say, and this is very intentional from David, and Ed, and Chris, our founders, is we have a culture at NewBank, which is the most alive in our employees' minds that I've ever experienced. Having worked at Google, and Facebook, and other places like that, I would bet that probably 80% to 90% of our employees could recite the five values to you if you stop them in the hall. (00:08:29): It's not just on the wall somewhere. And the first of those values is a very peculiar phrase, set of words strung together. We want our customers to love us fanatically. And I remember when I interviewed at NewBank for the first time, and actually flew down to Sao Paulo, I remember seeing that phrase and thinking, "These are my guys. These guys are taking this seriously." And a lot of my interview process from my side was really vetting if that was real, or if that was a sign on the wall. So you start with the intent that you are going to make your customers love you. (00:09:10): And there are a million reasons, operational, convenience, short-term financial viability, which is a real thing when you're a venture-funded startup. Any number of reasons why you can compromise those things on the edges, and in a decision day to day, minute to minute, "We can cut the edges, cut the corner here on that." And look, I don't think we have been perfect on that, but we try very hard. And when there are hard decisions to be made, we bias in favor of the customer. The customer's love, will they want to tell their friends, and neighbors, and family about it? And so I think that's the heart of it. (00:09:56): Once you get those things right, the deep pain point, and a culture that is maniacal about making your customers fanatical, then you start to do the trade craft of product development. You make sure that you focus on customer discovery before you start building. You make sure that that discovery is focused not simply on asking the customer, but on innovating on their behalf. You make sure that you take techniques from all over the place, from Procter and Gamble, to Google, to you name it, of maybe you can't ask the customer to tell you what massive new innovation they would love. You've got to observe them, and find their pain points even when they aren't noticing it. (00:10:49): And then as you build, you commit to measuring whether they in fact love the product, not fooling yourself about that. And iterating like crazy over and over and over again until you get it just right. So those are some of the principles, but I think the trade craft follows the focus on finding a real deeply held, emotionally held pain point, and a culture that says, that's your North Star.
turns.zh:
是的，我认为有几个基本要素能促成这一目标。需要说明的是，其中许多举措早在五年前我加入公司之前就已存在，但这个故事仍令人惊叹，也正是它激励我加入了这家公司。不过首先，我想说要深入挖掘并精准触及客户痛点。巴西的大型传统银行曾是全球盈利能力最强的银行之一，但它们同样饱受公众厌恶。（00:07:20）我个人对此深有体会。20年前，我在圣保罗为客户做咨询项目。有一天，我和客户（也是我的好友）一起去圣保罗的Classic Churrasque Korea餐厅用餐，路过他银行的分行时正好遇到红灯。他说那是他的银行，他很讨厌它。这事至今令我难忘。20年后，当David首次联系我时，这段经历仍历历在目。这说明我们确实触及了深层痛点，这里暂且不详解具体原因。但第二点至关重要——这也是David、Ed和Chris等创始人刻意营造的文化。在NewBank，员工对公司价值观的认同度是我见过最高的之一。曾在谷歌、Facebook等公司工作过的人可能会猜测，80%至90%的员工都能随口背出我们的五大价值观。这些价值观不只是挂在墙上装饰。其中首条价值观是一句独特的组合词："我们要让客户疯狂地爱上我们。"第一次面试时，我飞到圣保罗参加面试，看到这句话后心想："这些人就是我要找的伙伴。他们是认真对待这件事的。"整个面试过程，我都在验证这是否是真心实意，还是挂在墙上的装饰。所以你得从一开始就坚信，要让客户爱上你。这背后有无数理由——运营效率、便利性、短期财务可行性（对于风投支持的初创公司而言确实如此）。任何时候你都可能在边缘妥协，在日常决策中权衡利弊，比如"我们可以削减成本，偷工减料"。但我认为我们在这方面做得并不完美，但我们一直在努力。当面临艰难抉择时，我们总是偏向客户。客户是否会爱上它？他们是否愿意向朋友、邻居和家人推荐？我认为这才是关键所在。（00:09:10）一旦解决了深层痛点，并建立起以让客户疯狂喜爱为核心的文化，你就需要掌握产品开发的技巧。首先要在开发前专注于客户探索，确保探索不仅仅是询问客户，而是为他们创新。借鉴宝洁、谷歌等公司的经验，当你无法直接询问客户他们想要什么重大创新时，你必须观察他们，发现他们未曾注意到的痛点。（00:10:49）在开发过程中，你必须持续衡量客户是否真的喜爱产品，绝不自欺欺人。并反复进行迭代优化。
不断地进行迭代，直到你把它做得尽善尽美。以上就是一些基本原则，但我认为产品设计的核心在于，找到一个深深根植于用户心中的情感痛点，并在企业文化中确立这一痛点，将其视为企业的发展方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. There's so many threads there I'm going to follow, first of all, I want to go back to the values. So you said there's five, you mentioned one. Can you just quickly share the rest?
turns.zh: 太棒了。那里有好多帖子，我打算先通读一遍。首先，我想回归一下价值观。你提到有五个价值观，现在已经说了一个，能不能快速分享一下剩下的几个？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: The five, I'll mention them in the order that most resonate with me. First, we want our customers to love us fanatically. Second, we are hungry and we challenge the status quo. Third, we build strong and diverse teams. Fourth, we pursue smart efficiency. And one that is in many ways underlying all of it is, we think and act like owners, not renters. We do what is right even when no one is telling us to do it. And we have many instances of our employees taking that degree of extreme ownership as they build products and get them launched.
turns.zh: 这五个价值观，我会按照对我触动最深的顺序来分享。首先，我们希望客户疯狂地爱我们。其次，我们要有饥饿感，敢于挑战现状。第三，我们要打造强大且多元化的团队。第四，我们要追求智慧型效率。最后，贯穿于所有价值观的核心是，我们要像所有者而非租客那样思考和行动。即使没人要求我们做正确的事，我们也要坚持去做。我们的员工在开发产品和推出新功能时，很多时候都会展现出这种极致的自主性。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Talked about, you index towards if you had to make a decision, we're going to do something people love. Is there anything more you could share about just how you operationalize this? For example, is there design reviews where just you come in, or your head of design comes in like, "Is this helping customers love us fanatically?" What's in the systems and processes of how you operate that allows you to build that other than just cool, everyone has to remember this, this is what we're trying to do.
turns.zh: 好的。回到如何打造让人疯狂喜爱的产品这个话题，你提到这是一条首要原则，开发产品时每个人都要牢记这一点。你还提到，如果必须做决策，就要优先考虑能让用户疯狂喜爱的产品。能否详细讲讲如何在实际操作中贯彻这一理念？比如，有没有专门的设计评审会，让你或者设计主管参与其中，评判某个设计是否能真正激发用户的狂热喜爱？除了口头强调，你们还有哪些制度或流程来确保团队始终牢记这一目标？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah, we do a few things. And again, I don't want to also overstate that we've achieved some nirvana. We honor many of these things in the breach sometimes, but we have a series of techniques that we've begged, borrowed, stolen from other places, some of which we've invented on our own. But some examples, we love the Amazon mock press release technique. Explain to me before we've put a single engineer on the project, not explain to me actually, explain to the intended customer why they should care. Because if you can't tell me in two paragraphs why the customer you're building this for should care, then there's still work to do. So that's one technique. (00:13:41): We do have product and design reviews several times a week where we're asking ourselves that question, why is this great for the customer? Why is this fundamentally different for the customer? How does this redefine the category that we are thinking about on the dimensions of quality, on the dimensions of complexity, on the dimensions of price, and usually on the dimensions of all three of those at the same time? And breaking some of the trade-off constraints that you often wrestle with, and seeing if that's possible, which isn't always possible, but we frequently reach for that and sometimes find it. (00:14:26): And then there are other things you do after you've built and launched a product, whether it's alpha, beta, or a later stage. The measurement stuff. And some of your previous guests have talked about product market fit and how do you measure? Actually, it's strange. I was sitting here in Silicon Valley for well over a decade, I landed in Sao Paulo when I first joined Newbank. And the small product team at the time is telling me about this thing called Sean Ellis score. And we recently had Sean visit us in Sao Paulo and talk to all of the product managers and designers. But we are amongst the most fanatical followers of his methodology anywhere in the world. We rarely scale a project, a product we've launched, until we know the Sean Ellis score and we know that it's hit a threshold that we find really compelling.
turns.zh: 是的，我们确实做了一些事情。再说一次，我不想夸大其词地说我们已经达到了某种极致。我们有时会在项目中践行许多理念，但其中一些方法是我们从其他地方借鉴、模仿甚至窃取来的，还有一些是我们自己发明的。比如亚马逊的模拟新闻稿技巧。解释一下，在我们投入任何工程资源之前，先别急着向客户推销，先向目标客户解释为什么他们应该关注这个产品。因为如果你无法用两段文字说明为什么为你打造这个产品的客户会感兴趣，那说明工作还有待改进。这就是其中一种方法。（00:13:41）我们每周都会进行多次产品与设计评审，在此过程中我们会反复追问：为什么这对客户来说很棒？为什么这对客户来说有根本性的不同？如何在质量、复杂度、价格三个维度上重新定义我们所关注的品类？通常这三个维度会同时被考量。同时，突破那些你常被困在其中的权衡约束，看看是否有可能突破——这并非总能实现，但我们会频繁尝试，有时也能成功。（00:14:26）在产品开发和发布后，无论是α版、β版还是更成熟的阶段，还有一些工作需要做。比如衡量指标。之前的一些嘉宾谈到了产品市场匹配度以及如何衡量。说起来挺奇怪的，我在硅谷待了十多年后，加入Newbank时首站就到了圣保罗。当时的小型产品团队向我介绍了一个叫Sean Ellis Score的工具。最近Sean还亲临圣保罗，为所有产品经理和设计师做了分享。但我们是全球范围内最狂热的Sean Ellis方法论追随者之一。除非我们了解Sean Ellis Score并确认其达到了我们认为足够理想的阈值，否则我们绝不会大规模推广已上线的项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you describe the actual score and the approach?
turns.zh: 你能具体描述一下Sean Ellis Score以及相关方法吗？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah, the Sean Ellis score is a really simple methodology used by lots and lots of companies that a gentleman named Sean Ellis popularized well over a decade ago. Which basically asks your customers at each stage, and at each stage you have a small number of customers, then a larger group, and growing over time. But at each stage you ask them, how disappointed would you be if this product went away? And what Sean has said is that if at least 40% of your customers are not very disappointed, not just a little disappointed, but very disappointed, he has essentially a three point scale. Not disappointed, somewhat disappointed, very disappointed. (00:16:09): If at least 40% are not very disappointed, you haven't reached product market fit. Now we've had to do some things in NewBank, Brazilians are a culturally happier group than the global average. So for us, our threshold isn't 40%, we've generally moved it up to 50%. I don't believe we have product market fit unless 50% of Brazilians are telling us they would be very disappointed, because Brazilians are inherently polite. And more polite and more optimistic than average, so we make our own little tweaks and adjustments. (00:16:41): But we find that to be very helpful. As a company, this extends beyond product, we are addicted to our NPS score. And we reach for world beating net promoter scores as a company, and product vertical by product vertical as well. And we are maniacal about tracking how we do. And again, we compensate for some cultural biases, and we make sure that we hold ourselves to a high bar. But there have been, for example, in Mexico, we've recorded an NPS when we launched the first couple of years of 94-95.
turns.zh:
是的，肖恩·埃利斯评分法是一套非常简单的方法论，十多年前由肖恩·埃利斯推广，得到了众多公司的应用。基本上，它在每个产品阶段都会询问客户，每个阶段的客户数量较少，随后逐渐增加。但在每个阶段都会询问：如果这款产品消失，你会有多失望？肖恩指出，如果至少40%的客户非常失望（而非轻微失望），他会将评分标准设为三级：不失望、有些失望、非常失望。（00:16:09）：如果至少40%的客户不感到非常失望，那么就说明尚未达到产品与市场的契合点。我们在NewBank遇到过一些挑战，巴西人相较于全球平均水平更为乐观。因此，我们将门槛提升至50%。除非50%的巴西人表示会非常失望，否则我们认为尚未达到产品与市场的契合点，因为巴西人天生比较礼貌，乐观度也高于平均水平，所以我们会根据实际情况进行微调。

（00:16:41）：但我们发现这非常有效。作为一家公司，这项方法不仅适用于产品层面，我们还痴迷于NPS评分。我们致力于在全公司层面、各产品垂直领域都打造世界顶尖的NPS评分，并对数据追踪如痴如醉。我们会克服一些文化偏差，确保始终保持高标准。例如，在墨西哥，我们首年推出的产品NPS评分就达到了94-95分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's absurd. I've never heard of that.
turns.zh: 这太荒谬了。我从未听说过这种方法。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah. Which is way better than we got in Brazil, but our NPS scores skew in the 70s, 80s, and occasionally 90s. And when they dip down even one or two points, that's a reason for alarm. And we try to figure out why and we try to make sure that we make the iterations. So those are the things we build in. Those are the things we build in.
turns.zh: 是的。这比我们在巴西的表现要好得多，但我们的NPS评分通常在70、80分左右，偶尔能达到90分。一旦评分下降一两点，就是需要警惕的信号。我们会追根溯源，确保及时优化产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad you got into this, I was going to get into how you measure this stuff. So what it sounds like is the Sean Ellis survey is used as you iterate and launch towards launch. And then NPS is maybe post-launch to see how people like the product.
turns.zh: 很高兴你能深入探讨这个话题，我正想了解如何衡量这些指标。听起来肖恩·埃利斯调查法主要用于产品迭代和上线前后阶段，而NPS评分则是在产品上线后用于评估用户满意度。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: NPS is post-launch. We also look at metrics like churn to make sure that we're not building a leaky bucket, and that's part of this viral customer acquisition loop that we've built. We want to make sure we're building products that are great enough that our customers will tell their friends, and we don't have to invest as much in marketing to drive our growth. And that only works if the customers you get you retain. I have built earlier in my career products that have leaky buckets, and that's a very frustrating treadmill to be on. So I am personally maniacal about making sure that the bucket doesn't have a hole in the bottom.
turns.zh: NPS评分是在产品上线后进行的。我们还会关注客户流失率等指标，确保产品不像漏水的桶。这是我们构建的病毒式客户获取循环的关键环节。我们要确保产品足够优秀，让用户主动推荐，无需过度营销来推动增长。但这一切的前提是获取的客户能被成功留存。我早期参与的项目就曾遇到产品漏水的问题，那种无止境的内耗实在令人沮丧。所以我个人对产品质量格外执着，绝不允许产品有漏洞。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in this Sean Ellis piece, which is really interesting because I think it's something a lot of people can adopt if they're trying to build products people love, and also that succeed. Is this a goal for every project? And I don't know the strategy, or the one pager. Or is it just implied, "Okay, we're not going to move past this gate if 50%, less than 50% of people are not very disappointed." Is that how it's operationalized?
turns.zh: 肖恩·埃利斯的这篇文章非常有趣，我认为对于任何试图打造用户喜爱且成功的产品的人来说，都值得借鉴。那么，这是每个项目的目标吗？我不了解具体策略或单页文档。或者说这只是一个隐含的标准——“如果50%或不足50%的人对新产品感到非常失望，我们就不会推进下一步。”这是否是实际的操作方式？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah, we basically operationalize it. We don't have it as a hard and fast rule that is in black and white, but essentially that's the question people know they're going to get in any product review that's a post-launch, post data product review is what's the Sean Ellis score? How do you know that customers love it? Not just like it, but love it to the degree that they're going to tell their friends about it. That's pretty baked in culturally at this point.
turns.zh: 是的，我们确实会这样操作。虽然没有明确写入黑白条款，但本质上这是每个产品回顾阶段都会面临的问题——即便产品已经上线并收集了数据，人们也会问：“肖恩·埃利斯评分是多少？如何判断用户是否真的喜爱这款产品？不只是‘喜欢’，而是‘爱到会主动向朋友推荐’的程度。如今这在我们公司已经深入人心了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is an incredible insight, and I think it explains a lot of the success you guys have had. Because that's a very high bar. Many people run the survey, and getting to past 20% is very hard. You have to be very disappointed if there's a new product they've never used goes away, that's a high bar. Most people are like, "Ah, whatever. I don't need this thing." And you're saying you look for 50% of people feeling very disappointed if this new thing they've never used before goes away.
turns.zh: 这真是个深刻的见解，我认为它解释了你们成功的诸多原因。因为这个标准实在太高了。很多产品团队做完调查后，很难突破20%的满意度。只有当用户对新产品（即便从未使用过）消失感到极度失望时，才会达到50%的满意度。大多数人会说：“随便啦，我又不需要这个东西。” 而你们却要求50%的用户对新产品消失感到非常失望。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah, that's right. There are several on the newer side of products that we're launching now we're at borderline 50, and my push to the team is what are the three, four, five things you need to build to really get decisively beyond 50? And what are the segments or cohorts where it is above 50, and what is that telling us versus the cohorts where it's lower than that? So we put a lot of analytical effort, and a lot of depth of thinking. We were in a product review several years ago, and our lead designer, whose ex Google and ex-Facebook, we were in a review together and the team was saying, "We think this is good enough for launch." (00:20:44): And he used the phrase, which both Chris and Kara, one of our co-founders and I have now adopted, which is, "Good enough, isn't good enough. Is it great enough?" Is it great enough? Because that's the bar, particularly for some of our ten-pole products, but we try to apply it largely across the board. A lot of companies, not just in Brazil or Latam, but everywhere, spend a ton of money on marketing. Their VC budgets, VC funding basically goes to Google and Facebook. And I've spent a lot of my career taking that money on board for Google and Facebook. But it is a much better scenario if that's a small portion of what you're doing, and the main portion of what you're doing is actually investing in making the product great that you don't have to do that.
turns.zh: 没错。现在我们推出的新产品中，很多都处于50%的边缘水平。我对团队的要求是：要想真正突破50%，需要重点构建哪三个、四个或五个核心功能？哪些细分用户群体或用户组的满意度超过50%？这与满意度低于50%的用户组相比，能告诉我们哪些信息？为此我们投入了大量分析工作，进行了深入思考。几年前的一次产品评审中，我们的首席设计师（曾任职于谷歌和Facebook）和团队成员一起说：“我们觉得这个产品已经可以上线了。”但他说了一句话，现在我、克里斯和联合创始人卡拉都深有共鸣：“‘足够好’是不够的，必须‘足够伟大’。” 是的，这就是标准。特别是对于我们的一些核心产品更是如此，但我们正努力将其推广到所有产品中。许多公司，不只是巴西或拉丁美洲，而是全球范围内，都会在营销上投入巨资。他们的风投预算、风投资金基本都流向了谷歌和Facebook。而我职业生涯的大部分时间都在为谷歌和Facebook争取这些资金。但如果这类支出仅占你预算的一小部分，而把主要精力投入到打造伟大的产品上，那情况会好得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of a project that comes to mind that was below that bar and then you pushed it above where you're like, "Here's the thing we were missing."?
turns.zh: 能否举个例子，说明某个项目起初未达标，然后通过改进突破了标准，让你感叹“原来我们还缺少这个环节”？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah, I'll give you one that we're wrestling with right now. We have a product called Assistente de Pagamentos, payments assistant. It's right now only launched in Brazil, we haven't yet launched it in Mexico and Colombia. Paying bills in Brazil is quite complex. There are four different ways, four different payment rails that different payments use. From the mobile payment system that has exploded in Brazil the last three years called PIX, that's become fairly world famous in the FinTech world, to more standard and some more archaic rails as well. (00:22:16): So if you're a customer, you've got to keep track of your bills like we all do. You've got to keep track of which rail, you got to collect your bills, you got to make sure that you pay them. And some of the rails actually aren't that reliable. So you've paid it, it doesn't go through. And the consequences for not paying a bill is getting reported to the credit bureau and becoming what is called negativado, having a negative mark on your credit report. And that can be a big deal for the average customer. And so this was a real deep pain point. (00:22:49): And as we launched the product in a Reid Hoffman style, if you are not embarrassed by V1 you've waited too long. As we've done that last year, we found that a very interesting pattern. We had a decent Sean Ellis score, borderline 40%, I forget the exact number, but basically in that ballpark. But we found that there was a small cohort of a customer base who had more than four plus commitments registered. And even more so within that small cohort an even smaller bullseye cohort who had more than four commitments on at least two of the four rails. And their Sean Ellis score hit 70% and we're like, "Okay, the key is we need to across these rails, not have them one by one. And we need to make it easy for customers to onboard multiple bills across multiple rails." And then the automation takes over and people see the real, benefit because there are ways ...
turns.zh:
是的，我来举个我们目前正在攻克的难题。我们的产品叫Assistente de Pagamentos，支付助手。目前它只在巴西上线，还没在墨西哥和哥伦比亚推行。巴西的账单支付流程相当复杂，有四种不同的支付方式和支付通道。从过去三年在巴西爆火的移动支付系统PIX（已在金融科技领域闻名）到更传统、更落后的支付通道，每个渠道都有其独特的优缺点。（00:22:16）所以如果你是用户，就得像我们所有人一样记录账单，分清不同支付通道的账单，确认支付成功。有些支付通道甚至不稳定，明明支付成功了却未到账。逾期未付的后果很严重，会被上报到征信系统，留下负面记录。这对普通用户来说可是大麻烦。所以这是一个亟待解决的痛点。

（00:22:49）我们按照里德·霍夫曼的理念推出产品——如果V1版本不让人尴尬，那就说明你等得太久了。去年我们发现了一个很有意思的现象。我们的Sean Ellis评分不错，勉强达到40%（具体数字记不清了，但大致在这个区间）。但我们发现有一小部分用户注册了四个以上的支付承诺。更特别的是，在这部分用户中，有更小的一群精英用户，他们在四个支付通道中的至少两个通道上都注册了四个以上的支付承诺。他们的Sean Ellis评分高达70%。这时我们意识到，关键在于跨越这些支付通道，用户不必逐一操作，而是让他们能轻松跨多个支付通道管理多个账单。接下来自动化流程接管，用户就能感受到实实在在的好处，因为确实有实现这种体验的办法……

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Patient takes over and people see the real benefit because there are ways. On the surface if you said to the average person anywhere, any sort of developed country, we're going to have a bill auto-pay, that's on the face of it not necessarily exciting, but if you build it right, it is actually a fundamentally different experience rather than incrementally better experience. And that's what we've done. We've systematically made dozens of iterations on the product to allow customers to in one go do multiple bills across multiple rails and make that tiny bullseye cohort that we had, segment that we had a larger and larger proportion of the customers who are trying, and by the way, that's a journey still underway. We have a whole road map for the next year of lots of small quality adjustments that we're going to make and we're seeing some great feedback. We're now over 10 million monthly actives on that product when we were struggling in the hundreds of thousands about 15 months ago.
turns.zh: 耐心点，再听听用户的真实反馈。表面上，如果你对任何发达国家的普通人说要实现账单自动支付，听起来并不令人兴奋。但如果做得好，它实际上会带来根本性的体验变革，而非渐进式的改进。这就是我们做的。我们对产品进行了数十次迭代，让用户能一次性管理多个支付通道的多个账单，并不断优化那个小精英用户群体。如今，相比15个月前数十万的月活用户，这个产品如今已拥有超过1000万的月活用户。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is a really interesting insight there of just using the score and survey to narrow in on who actually loves this the most and see if there's something there. Is that something that you generally do or is that just like, oh wow that came up in this exam?
turns.zh: 这真是个有趣的洞察，通过评分和调查来锁定最热衷用户，再观察其中是否有共通之处。这是你们常用的方法吗？还是说这只是在这次考试中偶然发现的？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: We do that fairly frequently. When we did our, we have a high income rewards credit card. It's called Ultravioleta. We went through a similar process where at launch there were many different customer segments, but there was one that really loved the product and it was not surprising. There were the ones where the customer spent enough each month that they got the fee waiver and then all of the other benefits that we had built in really resonated. Whereas if you're paying the monthly fee, those other benefits were not quite as exciting or didn't quite compensate. So we've done this several times and we've started recently combining it with trying to get very agile in getting that feedback from that bullseye segment. So we've told many of our product managers and designers over the last two years, don't worry about serving 1000 customers, taking three weeks, serving 1000 customers, getting a bunch of cross tabs. Even at the end of which it's very hard to read the real fine grain customer feedback. (00:26:27): So we just tell them, call 10 of them. Pick up the phone yourself. Don't ask a researcher to come up with a plan to go do the research to then summarize it, to then bring it to you, which has so many degrees of distance built in. You pick up the phone, call 10 of them and nine times out of 10, by the time you've made your fifth call, you could predict what's customer six, seven, eight, nine and 10 are going to tell you. And then you know what it is that is the gap or what it is that is truly resonating that you want to double down on. So we're constantly trying to iterate in small ways the ways to get really that voice of the customer straight lined in to the people who are building the product.
turns.zh: 我们经常这么做。比如我们推出的Ultravioleta信用卡，就是一款高收入奖励卡。当时我们也经历了类似的过程——产品刚推出时，有很多不同类型的客户群体，但其中有一个群体对产品格外青睐，这并不意外。还有一些客户每月消费达到一定金额后，就能享受免手续费优惠，产品内置的其他福利也深受他们欢迎。而对于那些每月支付手续费的客户来说，这些福利的吸引力就没那么大了。所以我们多次尝试这种方法，最近还开始将其与快速获取目标客户反馈的敏捷流程相结合。过去两年，我们一直告诫产品经理和设计师：别费力去服务1000个客户，花三周时间收集大量交叉表格数据，最终却难以解读真实的客户反馈。（00:26:27）所以我们直接让他们随机挑选10个客户打电话沟通。自己拿起电话主动沟通，绝不让研究人员设计方案、开展调研再汇报总结——这样中间隔了太多层级。只要打完第五个电话，基本就能预测第六、七、八、九个客户会说什么。然后你就能清楚哪里存在差距，或者哪些点真正能引发共鸣，值得深入挖掘。因此我们不断尝试以小步迭代的方式，让客户声音直接传递到产品开发团队中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this advice. I imagine as a PM that is extremely scary to go call a customer. Most people don't do that. By the way, do you actually operationally, is it actually a call or do you recommend the email? What do you actually recommend they do because,-
turns.zh: 我特别喜欢这种建议。作为产品经理，打电话给客户沟通实在太吓人了。大多数人都不敢这么做。顺便问一下，实际操作中，你们是直接打电话还是推荐发邮件？到底该怎么做呢？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: We literally pick up the phone.
turns.zh: 我们直接拿起电话打。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Pick up the phone.
turns.zh: 拿起电话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. Great.
turns.zh: 好的。太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Because you can get tone of voice. Brazilians and Mexicans are incredibly expressive. There is a degree of real fine grain sense that the statistics never tell you.
turns.zh: 因为你能捕捉到语气。巴西人和墨西哥人表达欲极强。有些细微的感受是数据永远无法传达的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: And it's very aligned with design thinking and there's a lot of literature around how this works well, and I wouldn't say we're doing it especially to the best practice scientific. We're just like, just make the call. Make it as simple, as unobtrusive with as little overhead as possible to make sure the voice of the customer is coming directly into the teams that are building.
turns.zh: 这和设计思维非常契合，有很多文献都提到这种方法效果显著。我不会说我们严格按照最佳实践科学方法操作，只是觉得直接打电话就行了。尽可能简化、低调，减少流程负担，确保客户声音能直接传递到开发团队中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jeff Bezos had this quote on his Lex Friedman podcast where if you have data and you have an anecdote, usually the anecdote is right.
turns.zh: 杰夫·贝索斯在Lex Friedman的播客中说过：如果你有数据和轶事，最后的轶事往往更准确。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: I love that. That sounds exactly right to me.
turns.zh: 我特别赞同。这听起来太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To make it even more tactical for the surveys you run, is there any tool you find? How do you actually collect this data? Is there anything interesting that you could share of just how to operationalize collecting this data?
turns.zh: 对于你们开展的调查，有没有什么工具推荐？如何实际收集这些数据？有没有什么值得分享的操作方法？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: We've used a series of tools, many of the main survey vendor tools, we still use many of them, but we don't standardize or find one that dramatically changes our life beyond the mindset of we are going to make sure that this product has product market fit before we scale it. One of the things I've seen throughout my career as a product manager and CPO, we live with it today at Nubank every month is the pressure on the line product manager to scale the product that the entire company, the entire executive team, the entire management chain has been counting on. We're launching this thing [foreign language 00:29:16]. We all wanted to scale. We all are very excited about it. We had the product review six months ago and we thought this is going to be amazing. And the pressure on that product manager to scale a product is immense and the job of the product manager in many instances is to say no. (00:29:35): And one of the things I try to say frequently within the walls of Nubank is we are not going to take a small problem and scale it because if we do that, we end up with a big mess. Something isn't working at small scale, no problem, especially if we have a strong hypothesis and a lot of ways of getting good customer feedback. We iterate, we iterate, we get it right and then once we get it right, scaling if you do it right in many cases takes care of itself because the customer is now excitedly telling their friends. (00:30:08): Whereas you can pour a lot of money and a lot of effort and when you have a big app like Nubank or places like Google and Facebook, you can make any product look great for months if not years because you have such a large customer base that you can always get them to try it with all sorts of basic techniques, but you're bouncing a dead cat. And then you've got a real big mess to untangle when the thing is much, much larger. So we try to be pretty disciplined about that. And that's a lot of what the Sean Ellis does is it bring science to some of that art of making that judgment call.
turns.zh: 我们使用过一系列工具，其中许多是主要的调查供应商工具，我们至今仍在使用许多这些工具，但我们并没有实现标准化，也没有找到能彻底改变我们生活、超越"确保产品符合市场需求后再扩大规模"这种思维模式的工具。在我的产品经理和首席产品官职业生涯中，我见证过这样的情况，如今在Nubank我们每个月都面临着这样的压力——让产品经理去扩大一个全公司、整个高管团队、整个管理层都寄予厚望的产品规模。我们要推出这个产品[外语00:29:16]。我们都想扩大规模，都对此充满热情。六个月前我们进行了产品评审，当时我们认为这会非常棒。但让产品经理扩大产品的压力是巨大的，而产品经理的职责在很多情况下就是说"不"。（00:29:35）：在Nubank内部，我经常强调的一点是，我们不会把一个小问题扩大化，因为那样最终会酿成大祸。小规模下某个东西行不通，没关系，尤其是如果我们有强有力的假设和获取优质客户反馈的多种方法。我们不断迭代，直到做对。一旦做对了，扩大规模在很多情况下就能自然而然地实现，因为客户会兴奋地向朋友推荐。（00:30:08）：相反，如果你投入大量资金和精力——比如在Nubank或谷歌、Facebook这样的公司——你可以让任何产品在数月甚至数年内看起来很棒，因为庞大的客户群能让你用各种基本技巧让用户尝试。但这不过是徒劳的努力。当产品规模大幅扩大时，要清理这个烂摊子就难上加难了。所以我们在这方面非常严格。肖恩·埃利斯（Sean Ellis）所做的很多工作，就是为这种判断带来科学依据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This point you made about it's the PMs job to push back and stop bad things from happening I think is such an important one. A lot of PMs are just told here, build this thing and they kind of know this is not going to work, this is a bad idea, but either they don't think they should be pushing back or they are not good at it. From the PMs you've worked with that are good at convincing and pushing back, like we should not do this yet, do you have any tactics or ways of communicating that you found effective for pushing back to, like you said, all this pressure that's coming down on them?
turns.zh: 你提到的产品经理有责任顶住压力、阻止错误决策，这一点我认为非常重要。很多产品经理只是被告知"把这个产品做出来"，但他们心里清楚这不会成功，是个糟糕的主意，但他们要么觉得不该反抗，要么不擅长反抗。从你合作过的善于说服、顶住压力的产品经理身上，你有没有发现有效的沟通策略，比如说"我们现在不该做这个"，以应对这种巨大的压力？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: One of the things I've learned relatively later in my career, I wish I'd learned it decade earlier, decades earlier even is how important culture is. And we talked about the five cultural tenets, but this idea of we are owners, not renters. You're an owner of that product as the product manager or the lead engineer or the lead designer or in fact anyone on the team. If you really don't think it's going to work, don't tell me what I want to hear. It's incumbent on you, it's expected of you as an owner to tell me the bad news and tell it to me early, even when it's convenient, even when there's a promotion at stake, these dynamics get very real very quickly then look, I don't think it's going to work and here's why, or it's not working and here's why, or we should kill it and here's why. (00:32:05): The second thing I would say is senior leaders at companies that have gone, especially startups that have scaled well, you usually have people who have been in that boat who have seen products that weren't working who have killed them or who have pivoted them pretty dramatically. And there's a lot of respect for someone who has a real clarity of thought and brings a high bar and is not simply going with the flow. So I think that's the main thing, is bringing that ownership mindset. And the second is bringing clarity and bringing data and understanding that most senior executives in whichever company are strong-willed and bring strong opinions. That's part of the job description. That's okay. It is your job whether product or design or engineering or whatever function as a leader to if you think you are practicing for one of those senior jobs, it's sort of let's say a mid-level, it doesn't come miraculously when you get a C-suite title, it's something that's going to be practiced. And it's something that is expected and I think that's not just a Nubank thing. (00:33:27): Certain cultures promote it better than others, but I think it's pretty universally important. And so I would just encourage people to try it, understand the trade-offs, understand the challenge, articulate the other side, but if you genuinely believe it's not yet ready to scale your products, at the end of the day, the big mess is a thing you're still going to owe and we're all going to forget that we told you to scale the thing. We're all going to still blame you at the end of the day. So you might as well bite the bullet earlier, pivot it when it's easier to do and it'll work out better in the end.
turns.zh:
职业生涯中我较晚才领悟到的一件事——真希望自己能早十年甚至更早意识到——就是文化的重要性。我们之前讨论了五项文化准则，但“我们是所有者，而非租客”这一理念尤为关键。无论你是产品经理、首席工程师、首席设计师，还是团队中的任何成员，你都是产品的“所有者”。如果你真心认为某个方案行不通，就别只说好听的话。要以所有者的身份，主动向我传递坏消息——即便时机不便，即便晋升机会在望，这种直面现实的勇气至关重要。（00:32:05）  
第二点建议是，成功扩张的初创公司的高层领导往往曾亲身经历过产品失败、砍掉项目或进行重大转型。他们深知，拥有清晰思路、设定高标准、不随波浮沉的人才最受尊重。因此，关键在于树立这种主人翁意识。同时，要清晰传达数据，理解大多数高管都意志坚定、见解鲜明，这是工作要求。没关系——无论是产品、设计、工程还是其他职位，若你想晋升至中层高管，绝非一蹴而就，而是需要日积月累的修炼。这不仅是Nubank的特质，更是普遍适用的准则。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to one more thread and then I'm going to go in a different direction. You talked a bit about talking to customers, finding innovative ideas, not just listening to what they're telling you. There's this whole skill of user research and interviewing customers and finding the pain point, figuring out what to build. Do you have any just, I don't know, tips or tactics or lessons you've learned about just how to do this well, how to uncover the pain point and then figure out what to actually build when you're interviewing customers?
turns.zh: 接下来我想再谈一个话题，然后转向其他方向。你提到了与客户沟通、挖掘创新点，不只是听取他们的反馈。用户研究、客户访谈、挖掘痛点、确定产品方向，这些都需要专业技巧。你是否有任何心得、策略或经验教训，帮助我们在访谈中更好地发现痛点、明确产品方向？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: I'll share a couple of thoughts, but I will tell you as a preface that it is arguably the area right now that I still wrestle with. I still think I, and we are not doing it as well. I've never seen it done quite as consistently great as it could be, and I think it's an area for where design thinking and a lot of the design function can help us, but it's very, very, it's one of the areas of greatest inconsistency that I see in product development. Having said that, a couple of things that I see that we sometimes do really well at Nubank and other times we miss on one dimension or the other. First off, per your Jeff Bezos anecdote, the anecdote usually trumps the data. And there are many times when I see teams that are doing very sophisticated analysis and they've sort of forgotten what the question is or what the conclusion they can draw from it truly is. So never lose sight of the value of the customer's words and the anecdote. That's one. (00:35:56): The second one that I believe very, very strongly in is I think teams often skip the step of clearly, very, very clearly working very hard to be super crisp in articulating their hypothesis. If you don't have a hypothesis, you're going to spend a lot of time researching, you're going to get a lot of data back, qualitative, anecdotal or quantitative and you're not going to know what to make of it because it's not either validating or invalidating your hypothesis because there isn't a hypothesis. So it just becomes an interesting conversation. (00:36:34): The third one is, I've got a hypothesis, I've got it really crisp and now the pitfall is I've fallen in love with my hypothesis. I'm a lawyer for my hypothesis. I'm not a judge of whether the hypothesis is right or not right. So I think that's another common pitfall. I've fallen into that one too many times to count. And then the last thing I would highlight is even when you have a strong hypothesis and you're actually in the mode of doing the research, observe more than ask questions if you can, ask indirect questions more than direct questions. Would you love this product? Right. Excited product manager has been working for two months on a design. You're searching for the problem more than the solution. You're looking indirectly and asking from multiple directions the same question rather than trying to find a yes, they love the thing you've been thinking about and swaying on for a long time. And if you can, observing is better than asking, although that's a tricky skill. Those are the things that I look for.
turns.zh:
我想分享几点想法，但首先要说明，这正是目前我仍在纠结的领域。我仍然认为，我们在这一方面做得不够好。我从未见过任何团队能始终如一地做到尽善尽美，而我认为设计思维和设计部门能在产品开发中为我们提供帮助，但这也是我见过的最不稳定的领域之一。话虽如此，Nubank有时确实能在这方面做得很好，当然也有时会在这或那方面出现偏差。首先，借用杰夫·贝索斯的例子，通常故事比数据更有说服力。很多时候，我看到团队进行了非常复杂的分析，却忘记了问题的核心，也忽视了能从中得出的真正结论。因此，永远不要忽视客户反馈和故事的价值。这是第一点。

（00:35:56）：第二点，我深信不疑的是，团队常常跳过清晰阐述假设这一关键步骤。如果没有假设，你会花大量时间做研究，收集大量定性、传闻或定量数据，却无从下手，因为这些数据既无法验证也无法否定你的假设，因为根本就没有假设。因此，这只会成为一场有趣的讨论。

（00:36:34）：第三点是，我有了假设，表述得非常清晰，但现在面临的陷阱是，我爱上了自己的假设。我成了假设的辩护律师，而不是判断假设是否正确的法官。所以我认为这也是一个常见的陷阱。我自己就多次深陷其中。最后我想强调的是，即使你有了一个强有力的假设，并且正在进行研究阶段，如果可以的话，多观察而非提问。直接提问不如间接提问。例如：你会喜欢这款产品吗？对。兴奋不已的产品经理已经为一款设计埋头两个月了。你现在是在寻找问题而非解决方案。你在间接地、从多个角度提出同一个问题，而不是试图确认用户是否真的会喜欢你思考已久却犹豫不决的产品。如果可以的话，观察胜过提问，尽管这是一项高难度技能。以上就是我关注的要点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With the hypothesis point, just to make sure people understand, your suggestion there is before you start talking to customers, doing your easy researches as a PM or just anyone on the team, essentially have a perspective on what you think is going to be true. Is that how you think about it?
turns.zh: 关于假设这部分，方便解释一下吗？你的意思是，在与客户交流、作为产品经理或团队成员进行初步研究之前，先对自己认为会成立的观点形成一个看法。对吗？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Exactly. Have a point of view on what you think the customer will say that will lead them to be really excited about your product. That way you will get very clearly eh or yes, bang the table excitement and you will know when you're getting that reaction.
turns.zh: 没错。先对客户可能对你的产品感到兴奋的观点形成一个看法。这样你就能清晰地听到“嗯”或者“太棒了”的回应，知道何时得到了这样的反馈。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of that just to make it even more concrete? Because I imagine many PMs are kind of feeling like they have to be unbiased and just like, let's see. Let's see if this is something we should do and I don't want to bias anyone against it. Is there a quick example of a hypothesis?
turns.zh: 能举个例子吗？因为我觉得很多产品经理总觉得自己必须保持中立，觉得“先看看吧，看看我们是否应该做这个项目，我不想让任何人对它产生偏见。”能举个快速的假设案例吗？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: One of the famous examples that's somewhat hypothesis related and somewhat observation related is the invention of the Swiffer from Procter & Gamble. Right. The people hate mopping and they will do it and they won't even realize how painful an experience it is because they've just developed the work arounds and they just deal with the burden. But if you observe very granularly what the problems are, then you can see where the problems are. And so if you bring a strong hypothesis to, that this is a real problem, even if customers aren't telling you it's a problem because they've just sort of gotten used to it. So that's one. (00:39:23): We have a hypothesis at Nubank. I'll give you one that's live. We have a hypothesis at Nubank that the joint bank account, I was doing some research on this just last week. The joint bank account was invented in the early, it's actually hard to say, but it was invented, depending on what source you believe, in the late 19th or early 20th century. And it was basically invented coincident with the social movement, sort of the women's liberation social movements before women in the US were legally allowed to vote, where women were not allowed to open a bank account without their husbands prior approval. That is the era from which the joint bank account that we still live with today came from. It's 120 to 150 years old. (00:40:17): I don't think it's surprising. Our hypothesis is it's not surprising that that artifact, that that product is not made for the modern customer, that it is easier for me to share a Spotify playlist with my wife or my daughter than it is for me to share a savings goal just mechanically. So we're going into a product development cycle that says there is a new social banking arrangement that is not about tweeting and it's not about social very broadly defined. It is about our financial lives are inherently social. And it is very hard to share with my spouse, with my kids, with my parents who might be helping me pay for my child's education as an example, use case. It's a very strong hypothesis. (00:41:18): But when you go into the research with the customer, you don't try to sell them. You try to see if they're experiencing pain points. And it becomes very hard when you're in and they say even something a little bit in the direction of what you hope they would say to not be like, jump in with a lot of excitement and then get into more of a sell mode with them and almost try to sell against your idea, push back against your idea, make the customer sell you in the interaction. And you play the devil's advocate. So those are the kinds of things we search for as we build products.
turns.zh:
一个著名的例子，既与假设相关，又与观察相关的，就是宝洁公司（Procter & Gamble）发明的Swiffer拖把。没错，人们讨厌拖地，但他们还是会去做，甚至意识不到这有多痛苦，因为他们已经找到了应对之策，习惯了将就。但如果你能细致观察问题所在，就能找到症结所在。即便客户因为习以为常而未必会主动提及，这也说明问题确实存在。这就是第一个例子。

（00:39:23）：在Nubank，我们也有一个假设。我举个正在实践的例子。我们认为联合银行账户存在问题。上周我刚研究过这个问题。联合银行账户最早发明于19世纪末或20世纪初，具体时间难以考证。它的诞生与社会运动相关——在美国女性获得选举权之前，女性开设银行账户需要丈夫批准。这就是我们至今仍在使用的联合银行账户的历史渊源，至今已有120至150年的历史。

（00:40:17）：我觉得这并不意外。我们的假设是，现有银行产品并不符合现代客户需求。比如，我和妻子、女儿分享Spotify播放列表比机械地分享储蓄目标要容易得多。因此，我们正在开发一种新的社交银行模式，它不局限于社交媒体，也不局限于宽泛定义的社交范畴，而是强调财务生活的社交属性。比如，如何与配偶、子女、父母（比如帮助支付子女教育费用）分享财务信息，这才是核心挑战。这是一个很有力的假设。

（00:41:18）：但在与客户研究时，我们不是去推销产品，而是去观察他们是否有痛点。当客户的反馈与你的预期有一定契合度时，切忌过度兴奋，急于推销自己的想法。相反，要保持耐心，引导客户进一步阐述痛点，让他们在互动中主动推销你的理念。这就是所谓的扮演“魔鬼代言人”的角色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That sounds like a great idea. I believe in this hypothesis. Today's episode is brought to you by OneSchema, the embeddable CSV importer for SaaS. Customers always seem to want to give you their data in the messiest possible CSV file. And building a spreadsheet importer becomes a never-ending sink for your engineering and support resources. You keep adding features to your spreadsheet importer, but customers keep running into issues. Six months later you're fixing yet another date conversion edge case bug. Most tools aren't built for handling messy data, but OneSchema is. Companies like Scale AI and Pave are using OneSchema to make it fast and easy to launch delightful spreadsheet import experiences from embeddable CSV import to importing CSVs from an SFTP folder on a recurring basis. (00:42:45): Spreadsheet import is such an awful experience in so many products. Customers get frustrated by useless messages like error online 53 and never end up getting started with your product. OneSchema intelligently corrects messy data so that your customers don't have to spend hours in Excel just to get started with your product. For listeners of this podcast, OneSchema is offering a $1,000 discount. Learn more at oneschema.co/Lenny. (00:43:13): I want to talk about strategy. I know that you have a very strong perspective on how to think about strategy and approach strategy. This is something that everyone always wants to get better at. Every PM is always told you want to build your strategic thinking muscles and this is really important to your career. I'd love to hear your take and how you approach developing strategy and your advice to folks.
turns.zh: 听起来是个很棒的主意。我很认同这个假设。今天的节目由OneSchema赞助，这是面向SaaS的可嵌入CSV导入工具。客户总想把数据以最混乱的CSV文件形式交给你，而开发电子表格导入工具却成了工程和支持资源的无底洞。你不断添加新功能，却仍有用户遇到各种问题。六个月后，你又在修复另一个日期转换的边缘案例错误。大多数工具都无法处理混乱的数据，但OneSchema可以。Scale AI和Pave等公司正借助OneSchema，快速轻松地打造出优质的电子表格导入体验——从可嵌入的CSV导入，到定期从SFTP文件夹导入CSV数据。（00:42:45）：很多产品中的电子表格导入体验实在糟糕。用户被诸如“错误代码53”之类的无用提示困扰，最终根本没法开始使用你的产品。OneSchema能智能纠正混乱数据，让用户无需在Excel中花费数小时就能顺利上手。本播客听众可享1,000美元折扣，详情请访问oneschema.co/Lenny。（00:43:13）：我想谈谈战略。我知道你对战略思考和实施有着独到的见解。这是每个人都想提升的能力，每个产品经理都被告知要锻炼战略思维能力，这对职业发展至关重要。很想听听你的见解，以及你如何制定战略，并给出建议。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: I will readily admit, I bring a bias. I spent almost a decade at the beginning of my career right after college working in a strategy consulting firm. Right. So I bring a bias, which is to some degree, certainly for the length of time I did it, an unusual background for a product manager. When I first showed up at Google, it took me a couple of years to realize my job was not to produce a nice PowerPoint, it was to ship code. And I was doing a poor job of that for at least the first 12 to 18 months. But I think there is almost a countervailing dogma in Silicon Valley or in tech companies more generally, that strategy is easy and execution is everything. And I think that's probably because there are a small number of companies that get the strategy right, but the legendary companies that we all know about not only got the strategy right, but then executed it really crisply. What we don't hear about are the companies that got the strategy wrong, never got even into the conversation and all of their great execution was multiplied by zero. (00:44:46): Great execution multiplied by a poor strategy is a waste of everyone's time. And because the strategy isn't clear, you can waste a lot of time executing years and years against something that was destined never to work. One of my favorite quotes from the Valley, from Kevin Systrom in the early days of Instagram, I heard him say it at a conference, this is pre the Facebook acquisition. And he was like, I don't know how old. He had just left Google. He was probably, I don't know, 20 some years old. He said, "We may not be right, but at least we are clear." And what I love about that is even if your strategy isn't right, and it will never be exactly right because no plan ever is, you will have a clearer read on if you are going off course because you have a very clear idea of what was supposed to be happening. (00:45:41): And so I think being very clear in your strategy is really important. You've had some great guests on the podcast. Richard Rumelt is one of my absolute favorites. He's written a couple of books, one called Good Strategy Bad Strategy, another more recent one called The Crux, where he does a great service to the world by even more than describing what strategy is, focusing at the beginning about what strategy isn't. Strategy isn't an ambitious goal, it's not an aspiration, it's not a set of financial outcomes. It is a coherent plan for how you going to apply your strengths in a leveraged way against a core important problem. And that's a very, very rough paraphrase of the way he thinks about the world. And I find that we often confuse strategy with a vision, a broad idea, a very, very broad, vague aspiration. Nubank strategy isn't we want to be the world's largest neo bank. We do, but that's not an interesting way to dimensionalize the problem. (00:46:55): In 2014, we had millennial, middle-class, urban Brazilians who hated paying credit card fees and were not able to get credit in the first place because they were too young and without a credit history. And we could offer them not just a lower-priced credit card, but a no-fee credit card, which was an emotional thing. That fee got people angry and we could do that because we were branchless and digital. Now that is a coherent description of a very specific problem for a very specific set of customers with a very specific solution based on a very specific advantage. By the way, all of this predated my, this has got nothing to do with me. I wasn't there. But that's what I mean. Strategy is very specific, it's very detailed, it's very locked in. And working backwards from that I think is really, really important. And if you get that strategy right, it informs the minimal set of activities you need to do to get...
turns.zh:
我得承认，我带有偏见。在刚毕业开始职业生涯时，我曾在一家战略咨询公司工作了近十年。没错，所以我确实带有偏见——至少在我从事这份工作的那段时间里，这种背景对产品经理来说确实不寻常。当我刚加入谷歌时，花了好几年才意识到我的工作重点不是制作一份漂亮的PPT，而是真正把代码发布出去。在最初的12到18个月里，我在这方面做得很糟糕。但我认为，在硅谷或科技公司中普遍存在一种反向的教条，即战略容易，执行才是关键。这可能是因为只有少数公司制定了正确的战略，而我们熟知的传奇公司不仅制定了正确的战略，还能高效地将其付诸实践。我们很少听说那些战略失误的公司，最终连参与竞争的机会都没有，更遑论其出色的执行能力能产生什么价值。（00:44:46）：出色的执行能力若基于错误的战略，那就是在浪费所有人的时间。由于战略不清晰，你可能会在多年执行过程中浪费大量时间，却注定无法达成目标。我最喜欢硅谷的一句话，来自Instagram早期的Kevin Systrom。他在Facebook收购Instagram之前的一次会议上说这句话，当时他刚离开谷歌，大概20多岁。他说：“我们或许不对，但至少我们思路清晰。” 我喜欢这句话的原因是，即使你的战略不完美——毕竟没有完美的计划——但只要你清楚自己的方向，就能及时调整偏离轨道的风险。

（00:45:41）：所以我认为清晰的战略规划至关重要。你的播客邀请了许多优秀嘉宾，Richard Rumelt就是我最推崇的人之一。他写过两本书，一本叫《好战略坏战略》，另一本更近的《关键所在》。他为世界做出了巨大贡献，不仅描述了战略是什么，更着重指出战略不是什么。战略不是宏伟的目标，不是愿景，也不是财务结果，而是如何以杠杆效应发挥自身优势，解决核心问题。用他的话来说，这就是战略的核心要义。我发现人们常把战略与愿景、宏大构想或模糊的抱负混为一谈。比如Nubank的战略不是“成为全球最大的新银行”——虽然我们确实想做到，但这不是一个有意义的战略维度。2014年，我们面向巴西千禧一代中产阶级城市群体，他们厌恶支付信用卡费用，却因年龄小、无信用记录而无法获得信贷。我们不仅为他们提供低价信用卡，还提供免年费信用卡——这是一个能引发情感共鸣的方案。这种收费模式令人愤怒，而我们能做到这一点是因为无网点、全数字化运营。这就是针对特定客户群体的具体问题描述，基于特定优势的解决方案。顺便说一句，这些故事都发生在我加入Nubank之前，与我个人无关。但这正是我想说明的——战略必须具体、详细，基于特定优势，解决特定问题。
思路非常清晰。由此出发，逆向思考至关重要。只要策略制定得当，就能明确你需要开展的最少活动量，以实现……

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: ... minimal set of activities you need to do to get traction and to win, whereas if you don't have that degree of coherence, you're trying to serve all the customers. Maybe we should go to Mexico prematurely. All sorts of things happen and your execution gets very diffuse, and you can't even tell why you're not getting traction across the company, whereas strategy allows focus and it allows a much more rapid read of whether your focused bets, your concentrated bets, are actually working. (00:48:36): You've had some investors on your podcast over the years, and they will tell you that concentration is what builds wealth, diversification is what preserves wealth. And you're a startup. You're not trying to preserve anything. You're trying to build something. It requires concentrated bets, not hedging. And because you're concentrating bets, those bets are high stakes. You need to be very, very clear on what bets you're making and why you think it's going to succeed.
turns.zh: ......要获得关注并取得成功，你需要开展的最少量活动。但如果缺乏这种连贯性，你就会试图服务所有客户。或许我们不该过早进军墨西哥市场。各种状况会接踵而至，你的执行策略会变得杂乱无章，甚至无法解释为何整个公司都缺乏吸引力。相反，战略能聚焦重点，让你更迅速地判断你的专注性投入、集中性策略是否真正奏效。（00:48:36）：多年来，你的播客邀请过一些投资者，他们会告诉你，专注才能创造财富，而多元化只会保住财富。但你毕竟是初创企业，不需要保守财富，而是要开创事业。这就需要专注性的投入，而非分散风险。由于专注于核心方向，这些赌注注定高风险。你必须清晰明了自己在押注什么，以及为何相信它会成功。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When you work with PMs on your team in the past that are trying to get better at this muscle and following this advice that you're sharing of strategy, what do you find most helps them build this muscle? Is it just doing it over and over and over and over? Is it reading good strategy, bad strategy, practicing it? What do you find is most helpful in helping you build this muscle?
turns.zh: 过去与团队中的产品经理合作时，他们试图提升这项能力并遵循你分享的战略建议。你发现哪种方法最能帮助他们锻炼这种能力？是反复实践？还是研读优秀战略与糟糕战略的案例？哪种方法最有效？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: One is taking it seriously. It's a little bit like what we talked about with Nubank's culture. First, you got to want the customer to love you fanatically as something that you value. After that, I think frameworks really help, whether it's Good Strategy, Bad Strategy, whether it's Play to Win from a relatively recent guest of yours, Christopher Lochhead, who I really admire, whether it's Where to Play and How to Win from Roger Martin, which is a phenomenal book about-
turns.zh: 首先，要认真对待这件事。这与我们之前讨论的Nubank文化颇为相似。首先，你必须真心希望客户疯狂喜爱你的产品，这才是核心价值所在。之后，框架性的指导资料确实有帮助，比如《Good Strategy, Bad Strategy》（《优秀战略，糟糕战略》），或者你最近邀请的嘉宾克里斯托弗·洛克黑德（Christopher Lochhead）的《Play to Win》（《以赢为先》），以及罗杰·马丁（Roger Martin）的《Where to Play and How to Win》（《战略制胜》）——这是一本关于战略定位的杰出著作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: He's coming on the podcast in a few weeks.
turns.zh: 他将在几周后做客播客。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Is he? He's fantastic. And having those frameworks, all of which in many ways, if you synthesize them, are getting at the same thing around focus, around a clear understanding of the customer, around not trying to be in the words that we literally have on Nubank coffee mugs, "We're not trying to be incrementally better. We are trying to be fundamentally different." These are all very similar ideas expressed in slightly different ways. (00:50:26): Once you understand the frameworks and you distill them, then it's about practicing them and practicing them is scary. Hedging is appealing. Hedging means you don't have to make choices. Hedging sounds smart. Concentrating all your bets is the thing that desperate people do, and startups are desperate entities because they're burning cash in almost every instance. But successful startups, the ones that become profitable... I'm very wary, given the places I've worked, of the successful company with one or two monster products, and Nubank is now in that fortunate position, that starts to get conservative, that starts to forget that focus, concentration, customer obsession are every bit as important, that even though the company won't go bankrupt if products three, four, five and six don't succeed because products one and two are monster cashflow drivers, that's a slow path to death. (00:51:37): And so practicing that discipline and having, and I use this word very intentionally, having the courage to make those hard choices and to concentrate the bets, which goes against, by the way, a lot of what's taught in business school and a lot of MBAs is really important, and then it's a matter of you get better the more you do it and you get more practiced and more grooved and more principled in how you get to a methodology the more you do it.
turns.zh:
是吗？他太棒了。而那些框架，从很多方面看，如果你把它们综合起来，都在围绕着专注力、对客户的清晰理解，以及不试图做那些我们印在Nubank咖啡杯上的口号上的事——“我们不追求渐进式改进，我们要实现根本性变革”——这些都是用略有不同的方式表达的非常相似的理念。（00:50:26）：一旦你理解了这些框架并将它们提炼出来，接下来就是实践它们，而实践是件令人害怕的事。犹豫不决很诱人。犹豫意味着你不必做出选择。犹豫听起来很明智。但把所有赌注集中在一起，是绝望之人会做的事，而初创公司本质上就是绝望的实体，因为它们几乎在每个情况下都在烧钱。但成功的初创公司，那些盈利的公司……鉴于我曾工作过的那些地方，我对那些拥有一两个拳头产品的成功公司心存警惕，而Nubank现在正处于这个幸运的位置。它开始变得保守，开始忘记专注力、集中精力、以客户为核心这些同样重要的理念。即使产品三、四、五、六不成功，因为产品一、二是现金流的引擎，公司也不会破产，但这是一条通往死亡的缓慢之路。
（00:51:37）：所以，践行这种纪律，拥有——我特意用这个词——拥有做出那些艰难选择的勇气，并集中赌注，这与商学院和许多MBA课程所教授的内容背道而驰，但这非常重要。然后，你做得越多，就会越擅长，你会越熟练，越有原则，越能形成一种方法论。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Did you say the mugs at Nubank say, "Be fundamentally different"?
turns.zh: 你刚刚说Nubank的杯子上写着“要与众不同”吗？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: The product team, a little over a year ago we put together some schwag, which was fundamentally ... I have a mantra within the company since roughly the time I joined, which is, "We're in the business of being fundamentally different, not incrementally better." Again, it goes back to only fundamentally different, gets customers to tell their friends. Incrementally better. (00:52:46): And by the way, there are certain features ... I don't want to overstate the case ... There are certain features where you're in the incrementally better business. Not every single thing of the hundred things you launch in a year can be fundamentally different, but we're searching for those anchors that are going to be fundamentally different all the time around which you build some sustaining innovation as well, but we are in the fundamentally different business, not the incrementally better business.
turns.zh: 大约一年前，我们的产品团队制作了一些赠品，基本上是……自从我加入公司以来，我在公司内部一直秉持这样一个信念：“我们从事的是彻底变革的业务，而不是渐进式改进。”再说一次，关键在于只有彻底变革，才能让客户去口口相传。渐进式改进……（00:52:46）：顺便说一下，确实有某些功能……我不想夸大其词……有些功能属于渐进式改进的范畴。一年内推出的上百个产品中，并非每个都能彻底变革，但我们一直在寻找那些始终能带来彻底变革的锚点，在此基础上构建可持续创新的业务，但我们从事的是彻底变革的业务，而不是渐进式改进的业务。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that, and that's a great segue to where I wanted to go, which is I know you're a big fan of category design. You mentioned Christopher Lochhead, former guest. This is actually one of the more common debates on this podcast of do people believe in we should be creating our own category or should we not? Is that a terrible idea? Is it a good idea? It feels like you're in the camp of this is actually very good and important. I'd love to hear your perspective and also just how Nubank did this.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点，这也正是我想谈论的方向。我知道你非常喜欢品类设计。你提到了前嘉宾克里斯托弗·洛克黑德。这实际上是这个播客中最常见的争论之一：人们是否应该相信我们应该创造自己的品类，还是不应该？这是个糟糕的想法吗？是个好主意吗？感觉你属于支持这一观点的阵营，认为这确实非常重要。我很想听听你的看法，以及Nubank是如何做到这一点的。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: You know Lenny, literally earlier in this week, I was listening to your podcast with I believe it was Todd Jackson, ex Gmail product leader and now venture capitalist, and you guys had a very interesting discussion about it, and I think he took largely the other side of the argument that you go in a category where customers are already spending money. And it's hard to argue with that fairly robust logic. (00:54:03): I will tell you how I think about it. It forced me to think about where are the nuances in how I believe. I think overall, particularly at a company level, successful companies are typically in the fundamentally different business. They're in the new category business. Google was in the new category business. Netflix, Airbnb, you can go down the long list, Salesforce, et cetera, et cetera. That's really important. (00:54:31): In Nubank's case, we were the first, and actually, it's not that important that we were the first, but we were very intentionally trying to build a branchless bank based on the rise of the smartphone in Brazil and Latin America at that time, the sort of rapid inflection, and a branchless bank that could bring, as David likes to say, put a bank branch in your pocket, where at the time access was the big problem, and that you could do that on a digital cost structure that allowed you to essentially disruptively price across the board was the thing that led to the massive wave of success, multiplied by, unlike almost everywhere else in the world, including in the US where the answer was, "We're going to do the bank account first." Nubank's answer was, "No, we're going to do credit first and credit is 10 times harder and 100 times more risky," because you get credit wrong as a young company that doesn't know how to do it yet, you've blown everything up. The money's never coming back. Those two, again, concentrated bets, defining a new category, were I think the key to our success. (00:55:56): Now, there are times when you're trying to go into an adjacent market. We've recently gone into a market called Consignado in Brazil, which is secured lending for government employees. Very stable job, easier to underwrite against their salary at a much lower interest rate. That's a market that's existed for a couple of decades in Brazil, and our job was to go in there, and we believe we built something that is fundamentally different. It wasn't digital. It went through middlemen. We built it D to C, and we've been able to undercut the pricing pretty dramatically. (00:56:38): So even within an established category, we've tried to build a fundamentally different experience, but there are also times when, look, it's not quite me too, but the differentiation's a bit more incremental. But at the company level, I think it's absolutely imperative to be designing your own category so you can then dominate it and defining your own category. And even when you're entering a place where customers are spending money, I think going in with a mindset that says, "This is going to be a bit better," and I think Todd would probably agree with this, given the way he described it, you should try to be reinventing that category, even if you're not inventing that category.
turns.zh:
莱尼，你知道吗，就在本周早些时候，我听了你和托德·杰克逊的播客。托德曾是Gmail的产品负责人，现在是风险投资家，你们就这个话题展开了非常有趣的讨论。我觉得他基本上持相反观点，即进入一个客户已经在消费的领域是危险的。这种逻辑相当有说服力。
（00:54:03）：我来谈谈我的看法。这迫使我思考我所信奉的理念的细微差别。我认为总体而言，特别是在公司层面，成功的公司通常处于完全不同的业务领域。他们开创的是新类别业务。谷歌就属于新类别业务。Netflix、Airbnb，类似的例子还有Salesforce等等。这点非常重要。
（00:54:31）：以Nubank为例，我们是先行者，但先行者身份本身并不重要。关键在于，我们有意在巴西和拉丁美洲智能手机快速普及的背景下，打造一家无网点银行。正如大卫常说的，“把银行分支机构装进口袋”。当时获取金融服务是最大的难题，而我们能以数字化成本结构实现颠覆性定价，这正是我们成功的核心所在。与此不同的是，美国等多数地区的策略是“先做银行账户”，而Nubank选择“先做信贷”，因为信贷业务对初创公司而言难度系数是十倍、风险系数是百倍。若信贷业务出错，后果不堪设想。
（00:55:56）：有时候我们会尝试进入相邻市场。比如我们最近进军巴西的Consignado市场，即面向政府雇员的担保贷款业务。这些雇员就业稳定，基于其工资进行风险评估的难度较低，利率也更低。这项业务在巴西已有数十年历史，我们的目标是打造出与众不同的产品。它并非数字化服务，而是通过中介机构实现D-to-C模式，并成功大幅压低了定价。
（00:56:38）：即便在成熟类别中，我们也努力打造与众不同的体验。但有时差异化只是渐进式的。从公司层面而言，我认为设计专属品类至关重要，这样才能主导市场。即使进入客户已有消费习惯的领域，也要秉持“我们能做得更好”的心态。我相信托德会认同这种观点，毕竟他在播客中也如此描述——我们应该重塑品类，甚至创造全新品类。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I like this battle we're forming here of people on two sides of this debate, and I'm excited to see where it goes over time. It feels like the do not create a category side is winning so far in terms of volume, but there's a lot of passion from this other side.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我喜欢这场辩论双方交锋的氛围，期待未来能看到更多精彩。就目前而言，“不创造新品类”阵营在数量上占优，但另一方的热情同样高涨。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: I'm happy to be on the contrarian side.
turns.zh: 很高兴能站在反主流立场上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, there's a few more things I want to touch on before we wrap up. It feels like Nubank is one of the historically most successful companies launching new business lines. I think you guys are maybe like 10 years old, and how many products slash business lines are there at this point?
turns.zh: 好的，在结束之前，我还想再谈几点。这感觉Nubank是历史上最成功的推出新业务线的公司之一。我想你们公司成立才10年左右，现在有多少产品或业务线呢？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: It depends on how you categorize it, but I would say we have roughly a dozen to 20 core product lines.
turns.zh: 这得看你怎么分类，但我会说我们大约有12到20条核心产品线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that's wild.
turns.zh: 好吧，这真是太疯狂了。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Our story started as, we were a Brazilian credit card monoliner in an app and all the rest of it. Around the time, slightly before, but around the time I joined the phase two of the company, the mandate of what we were trying to do, which has really been the story of the last five years, was we were going to go from a Brazilian credit card company to a full solution Latin American bank, which meant we launched five new products. We launched a bank account, which allowed us to go from being a secondary banking relationship to increasingly a primary banking relationship. About half of our 90 plus million customers, we are the primary relationship. We built a lending product, we built an investments product, we built an insurance product, we built a series of small business products. (00:58:53): While we were doing that, we were also making the leap to prove, despite a lot of skepticism, that our business model was exportable and not a unique Brazilian phenomenon. So we launched into Mexico and launched into Colombia and now we are starting to take the full suite of products and go beyond credit card in Mexico and Colombia as well. (00:59:16): So depending on how you look at that matrix, we are a dozen plus products and we're working on the phase three of our products, which is moving beyond financial services. We've launched an e-commerce marketplace within our app, which is perhaps a bit counterintuitive if you're coming from the US. And we're also envisioning a world where banking is, again, to use the phrase that we love at Nubank, fundamentally different than it has been in the last 100 years. And we believe that social technology, self-driving and AI technologies can build a just completely different experience, where we're not building a bank branch and putting it in your pocket. We're building a personal banker, which today, I don't know, 10 million people around the world have access to and you got to have a lot of money to do it. (01:00:13): We believe that job can be democratized ultimately to all eight billion people on the planet, and we believe it can be done better for those eight billion even than the 10 million are getting today. But that's a lot of work, and that's, to use Christopher Lochhead and his co-author's language, that's the new category that we are trying to define over on a global basis.
turns.zh: 我们的发展历程是这样的，我们最初是一家巴西的信用卡公司，后来转型为应用程序等形式。大约在我加入公司第二阶段前后（时间稍早一点），我们的使命是从一家巴西信用卡公司发展成为一家全方位的拉丁美洲银行，这意味着我们推出了五款新产品。我们推出了银行账户，这使我们从次级银行关系转变为越来越多的主级银行关系。我们90多万客户中约有一半是我们的主级客户。我们开发了贷款产品、投资产品、保险产品，还开发了一系列小企业产品。（00:58:53）：在做这些的同时，我们还在努力证明，尽管面临诸多质疑，我们的商业模式是可以输出的，并非巴西特有的现象。因此，我们进军墨西哥和哥伦比亚市场，现在我们正开始在墨西哥和哥伦比亚将全套产品推向市场，超越信用卡业务。（00:59:16）：所以根据你如何看待这个矩阵，我们有十几种产品，并且我们正在开发第三阶段的产品，旨在超越金融服务领域。我们在应用程序内推出了电子商务市场，如果你来自美国，可能觉得这有点违背直觉。我们还设想一个世界，在这个世界里，银行业务——用我们在Nubank喜欢的说法——与过去100年的银行业务截然不同。我们相信，社交技术、自动驾驶和人工智能技术能够打造一种完全不同的体验，我们不是在打造一个口袋里的银行分支，而是打造一个个人银行顾问。如今，全球约有1000万人可以使用这种服务，但要做到这一点，你得有足够的资金。（01:00:13）：我们相信，这项服务最终可以民主化到全球80亿人手中，而且我们相信对这80亿人来说，服务质量可以比现在为1000万人提供的服务更好。但这需要大量工作，用Christopher Lochhead和他合著者的说法，这就是我们正试图在全球范围内定义的新类别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's going to be a tiny little banker to fit in your pocket, tiny little person.
turns.zh: 它将成为一个口袋里的小小银行家，非常小的人。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: That's it.
turns.zh: 就这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to follow on this thread, but before we get there, so in terms of adding new product lines and business units, watching how Nubank has done this, is there something you've learned about just how to do this well? I'm imagining there's a spreadsheet where, "Here's all the things we're going to do in the future. Here's how we're thinking about all the factors of all the new businesses we can launch." Is there anything there you've seen of just like, wow, that's a really smart way of thinking about the sequencing slash where to expand next that you think other folks can learn from?
turns.zh: 我想继续探讨这个话题，但在深入之前，先谈谈Nubank如何拓展新产品线和业务部门的问题。你们是否总结出了一些关于如何做好这项工作的经验？我想象应该有一份电子表格，上面列着未来要推出的所有业务，以及如何评估每个新业务的可行性。有没有什么具体的案例能让你们惊叹，觉得这真是高明的思路和决策顺序？值得其他公司借鉴的地方？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: I wish I could tell you that there was this predestined master plan that was so scientific. The reality is smart people around the table with a culture of robust debate and real candor about the pros and cons is how we went about it, and a constant re-examination of how things are going, what's going well, what's not going well, what's taking off, what's not yet taking off, what are the principles by which we're making these decisions has been important. (01:01:51): Some of these things are obvious. If you're running a bank, a bank account is probably a good product at some stage, but a lot of it in terms of sequencing and when we invest where, some of it's obvious, what's the TAM and where's the customer paying, but a lot of it is art and a lot of that resolution of the art and the debate. It comes from a fairly robust debate, so I'm avoiding your question. I have no good answer.
turns.zh: 真希望能告诉你，我们有一份科学严密的预先规划。但现实是，我们是靠一群聪明人，秉持激烈辩论和坦诚面对利弊的文化，在不断审视进展、评估成败、判断哪些业务能成功、哪些还在挣扎的过程中摸索前行。(01:01:51): 有些事情显而易见。比如，如果你运营一家银行，银行账户很可能在某个阶段是个不错的产品，但在序列安排和投资时机方面，很多决策需要权衡利弊。比如TAM（目标市场规模）和客户支付意愿这些基本要素固然重要，但大部分决策都需要权衡利弊，解决各种复杂的争议。这源于充分的辩论，所以我没法直接回答你的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a lot of complicated decision making, but I think what's interesting is, coming back to your very early lesson, is using the gate of is this hitting this 50% of people be very disappointed before launching feels like a key.
turns.zh: 这确实是复杂的决策过程，但我觉得你提到的早期经验很重要——在产品上线前用“如果50%的人会失望，那就别上线”这个标准来测试，是个关键。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah. That's the one thing is we try not to scale big problems, and so we try to solve our problems when things are small. Our ultra violetta are higher income, rewards-based credit card. We launched, it happened to be, I think it was July 4th, 2021 was the launch date, so it's easy for me to remember. We started scaling it two to two and a half years later. (01:03:04): In the meantime, we were in the lab figuring out where's the product market fit? Why is it not resonating? Oh, it's resonating with these guys. What do they particularly love it? Let's iterate there. And now we're at a point in the last six to nine months where we can start scaling aggressively, learning some of the credit dynamics that are different and reinventing some of those methodologies, and there's a second phase of scaling that will come. But yeah, one form of distraction we don't get into is fixing massive problems that we've overscaled before they were ready. That's a bit of an overstatement, but nothing's quite that clean, but generally true.
turns.zh: 是的。我们尽量避免在问题规模太大时就仓促扩张，而是选择在问题规模较小时解决问题。比如我们的超高端信用卡产品“Ultra Violetta”上线时，正好是2021年7月4日，我记得很清楚。两年半后我们才开始大规模推广。(01:03:04): 在此期间，我们在实验室里反复思考：产品与市场是否契合？为什么用户反响不佳？哦，原来他们特别喜欢这个功能！那就继续优化。现在过去六到九个月，我们已经能大规模推广，掌握了不同的信贷动态，重新发明了一些方法，接下来还会有第二阶段的推广。但我们绝不会在产品未成熟时就急于扩张。这有点夸张，但现实总不完美，但总体来说是正确的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to your thoughts on the future of FinTech and in LATAM especially, you talked about how the vision is essentially a banker in everyone's pocket. Is there anything more there? Just where do you think all this goes in the future in terms of FinTech banking for people in LATAM and then globally?
turns.zh: 回到你对金融科技未来发展的思考，特别是拉丁美洲市场，你提到愿景是让每个人口袋里都有一位银行家。这背后还有更深层的思考吗？你认为未来拉丁美洲乃至全球金融科技银行会如何发展？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: Yeah, there are a handful of principles, call them hypotheses, that we believe, and there are, I should be super clear, unproven hypotheses that will take years for us to prove out, and I'm sure there will be pivots along the way as we learn that things aren't quite the way we would've hoped at the beginning. But first off, the idea that banking should be holistic, that we need to provide a full solution across what we call the five or six financial seasons of someone's life, right? We spend, we save, we invest, we borrow, we protect, et cetera. And that's a lot of what we've been working on for the last handful of years. (01:04:52): So one is we want to be a full solution bank. Second, something we have started, we have had some real success in on the business side, we've made some mistakes on the technical side that we are iterating through is, we are trying to build, and some might argue I'm overstating a bit, but just to be clear, we are trying to build what we believe is the first global bank on a single code base. (01:05:22): I come from a world places like Google and Facebook, Google, my first product management experience. I was not allowed to launch unless my product was ready for 40 countries and 40 languages. I believe language number 40 was Finnish, so we were always making sure the thing worked in Finnish. And there are good reasons why ADVA, global online advertising, worked that way. It was a great principle by Google. (01:05:50): When you get into FinTech and into banking where the regulations are very local, where the stakes are much higher, that you serve the right 300 by 250 ad, there is a lot of pushback on that kind of, "We're just going to scale this everywhere," sort of mindset. And so how do you marry those two things? There are global banks like Citi or Santander, a lot of them have been built up through acquisition. A lot of them are on distinct code bases and technology infrastructures. We believe there's a lot of leverage if you can build a global bank on a single code base. That's another principle that we are trying to make real. (01:06:34): The third is that social mechanics around your financial life, not in general, not another WhatsApp, not another Twitter, and self-driving automation. Why do I have to remember to pay this bill every month? Why do I have to remember to save for my child's university education every month? Why can't I keep my life goals really well-organized? Which is almost impossible to do. My wife and I open up different bank accounts at different banks just to try to do that job, which is, talk about customer workarounds. How do we make the life life cycle of managing your financial life exponentially easier, leveraging these technologies and then using AI, which is an overhyped term right now, but AI to turbo-boost these tasks? (01:07:40): We have a phrase we've started using at Nubank, which I really like. David first introduced it. Customers everywhere around the world live harshly unoptimized financial lives. I think that's true regardless of income level, regardless of geography, regardless of sort of life stage of where people are at. If you have a young child, it is very hard to keep track of all the things you should be doing. You should be opening a savings account of a specific kind that stacks advantage in this way. (01:08:16): These are problems that should be solved and should be solved soon and can be automated and where insights can be brought to bear for customers who are not super sophisticated in their level of financial education, which by the way is almost all of us. Some of the people who think they're the most sophisticated are the ones who burn the most money in casinos that they call the stock market. (01:08:42): And so these are some of the principles around which we are the next phase. What if there were someone right next to you who could tell you what the smart move was to make today at this life stage? You've just had a child, you've just gotten married, you've just bought a house, you just want to remodel, whatever it might be. We think the technology is there or thereabouts to be able to do that. Why not have the company that reinvents banking come out of Sao Paulo, Mexico City, Bogota? Why does it have to come out of San Francisco, New York or London? We see no reason why it can't be us, so we're going to give it a whirl.
turns.zh:
是的，我们坚信一些原则——可以称之为假设——但必须明确的是，这些假设尚未得到验证，可能需要数年时间才能证明其正确性。在学习过程中，我们肯定会不断调整方向，因为现实往往与最初的期望有所偏差。但首先，我们认为银行业务应当全面覆盖客户人生中的五六个财务阶段：消费、储蓄、投资、借贷、保障等。这正是我们过去几年致力于打造的全方位解决方案。（01:04:52）  

其次，我们已在业务层面取得初步成功，但技术层面也犯过一些错误，目前正在迭代改进。我们正努力构建一个基于单一代码库的全球银行平台（有人可能认为我言过其实，但请明确理解：我们确实在努力打造首个基于单一代码库的全球性银行）。（01:05:22）  

我来自谷歌和Facebook这样的科技巨头，谷歌是我首个产品管理经历的起点。在那里，我必须确保产品在40个国家和40种语言环境下上线才被允许发布。我记得第40种语言是芬兰语，所以我们始终要确保产品在芬兰语环境下正常运行。Adva（全球在线广告公司）之所以能成功，部分原因在于谷歌的优秀原则。  

但当涉及高度监管的金融科技和银行业务时，情况就大不相同了。比如在Facebook上，只要按下“发布”按钮，产品就能覆盖全球。但在银行业，监管要求各国差异巨大，风险极高。如果想在全球范围内统一标准，必然会遭遇强烈抵制。如何平衡这两种需求？许多全球性银行如花旗、桑坦德等都是通过收购构建而成，各自基于不同的代码库和技术基础设施。我们坚信，基于单一代码库打造全球性银行才是可行的方向。这是我们正努力实现的另一个原则。  

第三，围绕财务生活的社交机制至关重要——并非指一般意义上的社交平台，也不是复制WhatsApp或Twitter的模式，而是自驱动的自动化服务。比如，为什么我每月都要记得支付账单？为什么要每月为孩子的大学教育储蓄？如何有效管理人生目标？这几乎是不可能完成的任务。我和妻子曾在不同银行开设账户，只为解决这些问题。如何利用技术和人工智能（当前被过度炒作的术语）极大简化财务管理周期？  

我们在Nubank引入了一个理念：全球各地的客户都过着财务管理严重低效的生活。无论收入水平、地域差异或人生阶段如何，这一观点都成立。例如，养育幼童的家庭，光是跟踪所有必做事项就已困难重重。针对这些问题，必须尽快找到可自动化且易于理解的解决方案，尤其适用于金融素养不足的客户群体。
我们当中有很多人都曾这样想。那些自以为最精明的人，反而是在被他们称为"股市"的赌场里输得最惨。（01:08:42）  
因此，这些就是我们即将进入的下一阶段所围绕的核心原则。假如此刻就有人站在你身旁，能告诉你在这个人生阶段该如何做出明智决策会怎样？你刚生了孩子，刚结婚，刚买了房子，想翻修房子——无论何种情况。我们认为技术已经具备或即将具备实现这一目标的条件。为什么银行业的创新公司非得诞生于旧金山、纽约或伦敦呢？为什么不能是我们呢？所以我们决定放手一试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I love all of this. I can't wait for this to be real. You mentioned AI, so I just have a couple more questions. You mentioned AI. We have a recurring segment on this podcast called AI Corner, so let's walk over to AI Corner.
turns.zh: 太棒了。我喜欢这一切。我迫不及待想看到它成为现实。你提到了人工智能，所以我还有几个问题。你提到人工智能。我们这个播客有一个名为"人工智能角"的固定环节，让我们移步到人工智能角吧。

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Usually I ask how you use AI in your day-to-day and your team, just like what are the tools and things you find useful to help your team operate with AI and tooling, but I'm also curious just how you're integrating AI into the product. You touched on this a little bit, but just how AI is going to supercharge the stuff that you're building.
turns.zh: 通常我会问你们如何在日常工作和团队中应用人工智能，比如使用哪些工具和方法来提升团队利用人工智能和相关工具的效率。但我也好奇你们是如何将人工智能融入产品的。你之前提到了一点，但具体如何让人工智能为你们正在开发的产品注入新动力呢？

turns.speaker: Jag Duggal
turns.en: We use some of the tools that everyone is using these days. Our ringfenced version of Chat GPT and some of the standard tools, we're using them in some of the obvious initial wave ways. How can we improve our customer experience? If you're fanatical about customers, you're fanatical about customer experience, and Nubank has always been that way. How can we make it even better while we're also making it more efficient? So we're doing all of those things as part of our coming up the learning curve in the last 18 or so months. (01:10:35): And then we're starting to think about what are the ways in which we can build AI native products. And I will not pretend to you that we've cracked that code, but a former boss of mine spoke a while ago, Fidji Simo, who's now the CEO of Instacart, but she was talking about the evolution when she was the product lead for Facebook Ads back when the big migration from the desktop to mobile was happening, and she talked about we needed to become mobile native.
